summary: The video is built around a model of the Konami 007121 chip: one register file, raster-driven interrupts, tilemap and sprite engines that fetch per scanline into line buffers, and a per-pixel priority mux that outputs a 7-bit colour code into the palette RAM, the way the chip's output pins would. It does not follow fastlane.cpp's screen_update (layer/sprite/layer draws with 40-pixel clip rectangles) or k007121's sprites_draw loop and offset tables. Register semantics are shared with MAME, as any correct core must share them, and the 051733 protection chip is a behavioural model whose register names and per-offset read switch look like MAME's handler. Below the chip level the design is behavioural RTL, not board gates, so the lean is moderate.

findings.signal: per-pixel priority mux producing chip colour code
findings.note: Each pixel goes through one tile-or-object select (obj_blank, tile_prio from attr bit 6 and the prio_en register bits, txt_line). The result is a 7-bit {pal_bank, tile/obj, 4-bit} code. MAME instead draws tilemap 0, then sprites, then tilemap 1 into a bitmap.

findings.signal: colour code indexes palette RAM directly
findings.note: The 7-bit chip output plus a half-select bit addresses a 256-byte palette RAM, read as two bytes per pixel. MAME builds a 1024x16 indirect pen table from the PROM at init time; the core does not.

findings.signal: layout mode replaces MAME clip rectangles
findings.note: The 40-pixel side column comes from the 007121 layout register bit (mmr[3][4]): different start positions, a second 'scores' pass in the tile fetcher, and a no_obj window. MAME's driver gets the same effect with hand-written clip[0]/clip[1] rectangles and a scrollx-40 adjustment.

NMI fires on rising edges of vdump[4] or vdump[5] (picked by mmr[7][4]). IRQ fires on the LVBL edge. FIRQ comes from a toggle flip-flop clocked by IRQ release. MAME uses a 16-line timer callback with a computed mask and frame_number()&1.

findings.signal: sprite engine scans the list per line, bit-level code formation
findings.note: Each scanline it reads attribute byte 4 first, then does a Y hit test, then reads the other bytes. Tile code bits code[3:0] are built from vsub/hflip bits. It stops on y==240 or a 384-pixel line budget. MAME uses a whole-frame loop with a 264-block count and the x_offset/y_offset tables {0,1,4,5}/{0,2,8,10}.

findings.signal: per-scanline tile fetch from VRAM scan address
findings.note: Tiles are fetched in raster order: a scan_addr built from h/v counters reads the attribute and code RAMs, and the code goes straight onto the ROM address with the row bits. There is no tile_info callback or cached tilemap. Bank bits are a per-bit mux of attribute bits selected by mmr[5]/mmr[4].
The meanings of the scroll, tile_msb, extra_mask/extra_bits, code9..12_sel, flip and interrupt-enable bits match MAME's ctrl_r use. Both a correct core and a correct emulator need these.

The register names op1/op2/op3/rad and the obj1/obj2 X/Y fields match MAME's local variables. The output is a case per read offset. Division, iterative sqrt search and an additive RNG are written as behavioural functions, with no chip-level structure.

findings.signal: CPU memory map and bank/IO decode
findings.note: The address compares, input port byte order, bank bits [3:2] and the 007232 bank bit 4 match MAME's map. Both must share this.
The even/odd register swap is an INVA0 parameter on a shared chip model, not a wrapper handler. It is functionally the same as MAME's offset^1.
